meta_title: Ratios and Proportions Grade 6 Practice + Quiz
meta_desc: Master ratios and proportions grade 6: simplify ratios, build ratio tables, find unit rates and solve proportions. Free 8-question quiz inside.
excerpt: Ratios trip up more Grade 6 students than any other topic I teach, and it is almost always because they were rushed. Here is the skill-by-skill way through it, with a ratio table you can copy and a quick quiz to check what stuck.
author: Sachin Sharma
content:
A student once told me the recipe called for 2 cups of rice to 3 cups of water, and she needed to cook for the whole family, so she ‘doubled the rice to 4 and kept the water at 3.’ The rice came out hard. That one kitchen mistake is the heart of ratios and proportions grade 6: a ratio only stays true if you scale both parts by the same amount. Get that idea to stick and the rest of the topic — equivalent ratios, unit rate, cross-multiplication — falls into place. Miss it, and every question becomes guesswork.

This is a skill-practice guide, not a chapter summary. I will walk through the four skills your child actually needs to grind on, in the order I teach them, with the exact mistakes to watch for.

Writing and simplifying ratios

A ratio compares two quantities of the same kind. If a class has 12 boys and 18 girls, the ratio of boys to girls is 12 : 18. Order matters — boys to girls is not the same as girls to boys, so always read the question twice before you write the colon.

Simplifying a ratio works exactly like reducing a fraction: divide both sides by their highest common factor. For 12 : 18 the HCF is 6, so it becomes 2 : 3. I insist students write the division out for a few weeks:

  • 12 ÷ 6 = 2
  • 18 ÷ 6 = 3
  • So 12 : 18 = 2 : 3, in simplest form

The one caveat that catches people: both quantities must be in the same unit first. To compare 1 metre to 40 centimetres, convert the metre to 100 cm, then write 100 : 40, which simplifies to 5 : 2. Comparing 1 : 40 there would be flat wrong, and it is the single most common slip I see.

Equivalent ratios and the ratio table

Two ratios are equivalent if one scales up or down to the other. 2 : 3 is the same relationship as 4 : 6, as 6 : 9, as 20 : 30 — you multiply both parts by the same number every time. A ratio table lays this out so the pattern is impossible to miss.

Notice the family from the failed recipe: 2 : 3 goes to 4 : 6, not 4 : 3. Had my student read across the row, she would have added a cup more water. A ratio table turns an abstract rule into something you can point at, which is why I reach for it before any formula.

Reading a ratio table both ways

The table is not just for scaling up. If a question gives you 8 cups of rice and asks for the water, you find 8 in the rice column and read across to 12. Working backwards like this is what separates students who understand equivalent ratios from those who only memorised ‘multiply both sides.’

Unit rate: the ratio with a 1 in it

A unit rate is how much of one quantity you get per single unit of another. If 4 pens cost ₹60, the unit rate is ₹60 ÷ 4 = ₹15 per pen. The trick is simply to divide until the second quantity becomes 1.

Unit rate is quietly the most useful skill on this whole list, because it powers real decisions. Which is the better buy — 5 chocolates for ₹100 or 8 chocolates for ₹144? Find each unit rate: ₹20 each versus ₹18 each. The pack of 8 wins. I have watched students who found ratios boring suddenly sit up when they realise this is how you spot a genuine deal at the shop.

Solving proportions: cross-multiplication and the unitary method

A proportion is a statement that two ratios are equal, like 2 : 3 = 8 : x. Grade 6 has two reliable ways to solve for the missing value, and I teach both because different students click with different ones.

The unitary method

Find the value of one unit first, then scale to what you need. If 3 notebooks cost ₹90, one notebook costs ₹90 ÷ 3 = ₹30, so 7 notebooks cost ₹30 × 7 = ₹210. It reads like plain sense, which is why I start here.

Cross-multiplication

Write the proportion as two fractions and cross-multiply. For 2/3 = 8/x, multiply 2 × x and 3 × 8 to get 2x = 24, so x = 12. It is faster once mastered, but I do not let students touch it until the unitary method feels natural — otherwise it becomes a rule they follow without knowing why it works.

SkillWhat you doExample
Simplify a ratioDivide both parts by the HCF12 : 18 = 2 : 3
Equivalent ratioMultiply both parts equally2 : 3 = 10 : 15
Unit rateDivide to make the second part 1₹60 for 4 = ₹15 each
Solve a proportionUnitary method or cross-multiply2 : 3 = 8 : 12

A practice routine that actually works

Twenty minutes, three times a week, beats a marathon on Sunday. My suggested split: one session on simplifying and equivalent ratios, one on unit rate with real price examples from your kitchen shelf, and one mixed session where the child has to decide whether a question needs a ratio table, a unit rate, or a proportion. That deciding step is where fluency lives — anyone can follow a method they were handed, but choosing the right one is the real skill.

Check what your child has learned

Try the free eight-question quiz below — it covers writing and simplifying ratios, equivalent ratios, unit rate and solving proportions, all at the Grade 6 level. Read the explanations together for anything missed. When your child is ready for longer written practice, the printable worksheet in the box below gives graded questions with a full answer key.

quiz.title: Grade 6 Ratios and Proportions Quiz
quiz.intro: Eight quick questions on writing and simplifying ratios, equivalent ratios, unit rate and solving proportions. Pick an answer for each, then press Check my score.
quiz.about: Grade 6 ratios, unit rate and proportions

questions.q: A class has 12 boys and 18 girls. What is the ratio of boys to girls in simplest form?
questions.explanation: Divide both parts by the HCF, 6: 12 ÷ 6 = 2 and 18 ÷ 6 = 3, giving 2 : 3.
Multiply both parts by 5: 2 × 5 = 10 and 3 × 5 = 15, so 2 : 3 = 10 : 15.

questions.q: If 4 pens cost ₹60, what is the cost of one pen (the unit rate)?
questions.explanation: Unit rate divides to make the second quantity 1: ₹60 ÷ 4 = ₹15 per pen.

questions.q: Solve the proportion 2 : 3 = 8 : x. What is x?
questions.explanation: 8 is 2 × 4, so scale the other part the same way: 3 × 4 = 12. So x = 12.

questions.q: To compare 1 metre to 40 centimetres, what is the ratio in simplest form?
questions.explanation: Use the same unit first: 1 m = 100 cm, so 100 : 40, which simplifies to 5 : 2.

questions.q: 3 notebooks cost ₹90. Using the unitary method, what do 7 notebooks cost?
questions.explanation: One notebook is ₹90 ÷ 3 = ₹30, so 7 notebooks cost ₹30 × 7 = ₹210.

questions.q: Which is the better buy: 5 chocolates for ₹100 or 8 chocolates for ₹144?
questions.explanation: Unit rates: ₹100 ÷ 5 = ₹20 each versus ₹144 ÷ 8 = ₹18 each. The pack of 8 is cheaper per chocolate.

questions.q: A recipe uses rice to water in the ratio 2 : 3. For 8 cups of rice, how much water is needed?
questions.explanation: 8 cups of rice is 2 × 4, so scale the water the same way: 3 × 4 = 12 cups.

faq.q: What is the difference between a ratio and a proportion?
faq.a: A ratio compares two quantities, like 2 : 3. A proportion is a statement that two ratios are equal, like 2 : 3 = 8 : 12. You use a proportion to find a missing value when you already know the ratio.

faq.q: Do both parts of a ratio have to be in the same unit?
faq.a: Yes, always convert first. To compare 1 metre with 40 centimetres you must write it as 100 cm : 40 cm, which simplifies to 5 : 2. Comparing 1 : 40 would be wrong — this is the most common Grade 6 mistake.

faq.q: Should my child learn cross-multiplication or the unitary method?
faq.a: Start with the unitary method — find the value of one unit, then scale up. It reads like common sense. Introduce cross-multiplication only once that feels natural, so it is a shortcut rather than a rule followed blindly.

faq.q: What is a unit rate and why does it matter?
faq.a: A unit rate is the amount per single unit, like ₹15 per pen. It matters because it powers real decisions: comparing two unit rates tells you instantly which pack at the shop is the better buy.
